title: The reverse-mex condition for subtraction Nim with s_3=s_1+s_2
statement: Consider the three-element subtraction Nim setup above, including the eventual period $p$ and the associated distance function $dist(w)$. **The reverse-mex condition.** If $s_3=s_1+s_2$, then the subtraction Nim satisfies condition $(a)$ of the reverse-$mex$ characterization: for every $\mathcal{P}$-position $w$ with $dist(w)=2m$ for some $m\in\mathbb{N}$ with $m\geq2$, $w+s_3-s_1\mathbin{\bmod}p$ is not a $\mathcal{P}$-position and $w+s_3-3s_1\mathbin{\bmod}p$ is a $\mathcal{P}$-position. This is a special-case prediction supporting the preceding characterization, based on the authors’ computer calculations; the source gives no proof or resolution.
references:
Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14321

Status: no resolution is reported in the source (as of May 2026).
source_name: Urban Larsson, Hikaru Manabe and Ryohei Miyadera, “A Subtraction Nim with a Pass”, arXiv:2605.14321 (2026).

progress.label: Open · solution reported
progress.tldr: A reader-posted claim of a complete proof has appeared, but it has not been independently checked, while published work covers only a narrower family.
progress.summary:
The problem asks whether the stated reverse-$\operatorname{mex}$ pattern always holds for additive subtraction sets with $s_3=s_1+s_2$. The primary paper reports computer-supported predictions for this setting but does not prove the general distance condition.

*[arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14321)*

**Known results**

- Larsson, Manabe, and Miyadera (2026) prove reverse-$\operatorname{mex}$ behavior for the narrower family $S=\\{2,4n,4n+2\\}$ with $n\ge3$, including a one-time-pass variant; this does not establish the stated general condition.


**Posted attempt**

A reader-posted argument claims a complete proof for every additive set $S=\\{a,b,a+b\\}$ and all relevant positions, including positions before the eventual-period tail. The argument has not been independently verified, so it establishes no confirmed resolution.

Current status (as of August 2026): A complete-proof claim is publicly posted but unverified; the general reverse-$\operatorname{mex}$ condition remains mathematically unsettled, while the narrower family above is proved.

*Caveats. The only purported general proof in the retrieved material is an unverified reader-submitted argument.*

solutions.body:
**Complete proof for all additive subtraction sets and all positions.**

Larsson–Manabe–Miyadera, [arXiv:2605.14321](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14321), Conjecture 2, considers the ordinary subtraction game with
\[
S=\{a,b,a+b\},\qquad 1\le a<b.
\]
Let \(p\) be any eventual period of its Sprague–Grundy sequence. For a losing position \(w\), define
\[
d=\operatorname{dist}(w)
=\min\{j\ge1:(w-ja)\bmod p\text{ is losing}\}.
\]
The conjecture asserts that whenever \(d\ge4\) is even,
\[
(w+b)\bmod p\text{ is winning},
\qquad
(w+b-2a)\bmod p\text{ is losing}.
\]

A prefix issue must first be handled: the conjecture includes losing positions before the eventual Grundy preperiod. We use the prior result of Bhagat–Larsson–Manabe–Yamashita, [arXiv:2601.18715](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.18715), equation (1), Theorem 3, and Corollary 4. Their equation (1) gives
\[
o_{\mathrm{wall}}(x)
=o_{\mathrm{sink}}(x+\max S+1)
\qquad(x\ge0),
\]
and their Theorem 3 proves that the additive sink sequence is purely periodic. Consequently the ordinary additive-game outcome has a global period \(P\):
\[
o_{\mathrm{wall}}(x+P)=o_{\mathrm{wall}}(x)
\qquad(x\ge0).
\]

Although \(p\) is initially assumed to be only an eventual Grundy period, it is in fact a **global outcome period**. For any \(x\ge0\), choose \(t\) so large that \(x+tP\) and \(x+p+tP\) lie in the eventual Grundy tail. Then
\[
o(x+p)=o(x+p+tP)=o(x+tP)=o(x).
\]
Thus all source-prescribed residue classes, including those represented by initial-prefix positions, have well-defined outcomes. Choose sufficiently large representatives so every subtraction below is legal. The ordinary recursion on the cycle is
\[
x\text{ losing}\iff
x-a,\ x-b,\ x-a-b\text{ are all winning}.
\]

Now fix a losing \(w\) and set
\[
z_j=w+b-ja\pmod p.
\]
The first queried position \(z_0=w+b\) is winning: its \(b\)-move reaches the losing position \(w\).

By minimality of \(d\),
\[
w-ja\text{ is winning}\quad(1\le j<d),
\qquad
w-da\text{ is losing}.
\]
The three followers of \(z_j\) are
\[
z_j-a=z_{j+1},
\qquad
z_j-b=w-ja,
\qquad
z_j-(a+b)=w-(j+1)a.
\]
Therefore \(z_{d-1}\) is winning, since its \((a+b)\)-move reaches \(w-da\). For \(1\le j\le d-2\), its latter two followers are both winning, so the entire recursion reduces to
\[
z_j\text{ losing}\iff z_{j+1}\text{ winning}.
\]
Backward induction yields the stronger exact alternating-strip formula
\[
\boxed{
z_j\text{ losing}
\iff d-1-j\text{ is odd}
\qquad(1\le j\le d-1).}
\]
When \(d\ge4\) is even, \(d-3\) is odd, and therefore
\[
\boxed{z_2=w+b-2a\text{ is losing},\qquad z_0=w+b\text{ is winning}.}
\]
These are exactly both parts of the conjectured condition for every \(a<b\), every permitted eventual Grundy period, and every losing position, including the entire initial preperiod.

The earlier sink-subtraction paper supplies global outcome periodicity; the alternating-strip argument above proves the distinct subsequent conjecture.
